data.about: Six little nodes, one lesson: at a loaded node the force polygon must CLOSE, and the shape of the polygon tells you everything. Where the members straddle the load, both are in tension or both in compression; where they lie on one side, one pushes while the other pulls; and where both are horizontal, no polygon can close at all — case e) is a mechanism, not a structure.

steps.caption: EX 1 task 4: six subsystems, each a single node with two members carrying F = 30 kN — close each force polygon and read off the two member forces
steps.title: The exercise

steps.caption: left: a) to f) — the same load every time, only the directions of the two members change (dash-dot: the load’s line of action)
steps.title: The six subsystems

steps.caption: left: a) both members rise from the node, b) both fall — right: in both the polygon is a symmetric triangle, so the two forces are equal; only their SENSE differs
steps.title: a) and b) — the load between the members

steps.caption: left: the horizontal member cannot carry anything vertical, so the inclined one must take the whole load alone — right: its force is much larger than F, and the horizontal member has to hold its pull back
steps.title: c) — one inclined, one horizontal

steps.caption: left: both members leave the node to the right — right: their horizontal parts must cancel, so one pulls and the other pushes
steps.title: d) — both members on one side

steps.caption: left: both members are horizontal, so neither can produce a vertical force — right: the polygon cannot close, the vertical gap F stays open whatever the member forces are. The node is a MECHANISM: it moves
steps.title: e) — no solution

steps.caption: left: identical members, only the load arrow is drawn above the node instead of below — right: the identical polygon
steps.title: f) — the same as d)

steps.caption: blue = compression, pink = tension, grey = no solution — the polygon’s shape carries the whole answer
steps.title: All six answers
